title: Define the sphere placement
shortPrompt: Mark top, bottom, left, right — plus paper margin.
text: Start by ghosting four light marks where the sphere will sit. These four marks define the size and position. Leave breathing room around the edges of your paper.

title: Measure left and right
shortPrompt: Use your pencil to compare distances from the center.
text: Hold your pencil horizontally. Measure from the center to the left mark, then to the right mark. They should be equal — if not, adjust.

title: Measure top and bottom
shortPrompt: Now check vertically — same pencil method.
text: Rotate your pencil vertically. Compare distance from center to top, then to bottom. Equal distances = a true sphere, not an oval.

title: Find the diagonal points
shortPrompt: Same radius — now on the diagonals.
text: Use the same pencil-radius to locate four diagonal guide points (NE, NW, SE, SW). These eight points together define the circle.

title: See the full framework
shortPrompt: Center cross + diameter + radius + 8 guide points.
text: This is the scaffolding underneath every well-drawn sphere. The cross gives you center. The eight points give you the curve. Trust the structure.

title: Cut with straight tangents first
shortPrompt: Connect points with short straight lines — not curves yet.
text: Beginner mistake: drawing a curve straight away. Instead, connect your eight points with short straight lines first. A circle is just many small straight cuts.

title: Refine into a clean curve
shortPrompt: Now soften the straight cuts into a smooth circle.
text: Once your tangent cuts are right, gently round the corners. Don't force perfection — let the curve emerge from the geometry you built.

title: Erase the cutting lines
shortPrompt: Clean up the outer edge — make the circle round and natural.
text: After cutting the sphere with straight tangents, use your eraser to clean away the leftover construction lines. This refinement makes the outer edge feel round, smooth, and natural — not geometric.

title: Cast shadow + sphere together
shortPrompt: The shadow is part of the same system as the sphere.
text: Draw the cast shadow at the same time as you finish the sphere. They're not two separate elements — they're one connected structure. The shadow grounds the sphere; the sphere casts the shadow.

title: Mark the terminator line
shortPrompt: Divide the sphere — light side vs shadow side.
text: As soon as the form is drawn, use the terminator line to clearly separate the light side from the shadow side. This single line is what makes a sphere read as three-dimensional.

title: Strengthen the terminator
shortPrompt: Go back to the terminator and darken it more.
text: Return to the terminator line and reinforce it. Strengthening this boundary is what creates strong contrast between the light side and the shadow side — and that contrast is what gives the sphere its volume.

title: Sharpen the shadow contrast
shortPrompt: Push the cast shadow darker — make the contrast clear.
text: Now move to the cast shadow below the sphere and strengthen its main contrast line. Making the shadow side firmly darker than the light side is what completes the illusion of form sitting in space.

title: Tone inside the terminator
shortPrompt: Stay inside the dark side — build tone within the terminator line.
text: Begin laying tone strictly within the terminator. Don't let your pencil cross over into the light side. This boundary is what gives the sphere its volume.

title: Strengthen the terminator
shortPrompt: Reinforce the terminator — keep it the darkest, most concentrated line.
text: Return to the terminator line after the overall tone is in. Push it darker — this line should always remain the deepest, most focused dark on the form.

title: Tone the shadow as one family
shortPrompt: Fill the cast shadow at the same time — same value family as the sphere.
text: Tone the cast shadow alongside the sphere, not separately. Sphere and shadow belong to the same value family — they should be developed together so they feel unified, not pasted together.

title: Anchor the sphere to the surface
shortPrompt: Strengthen the contact area — make the sphere sit on the table.
text: Once the cast shadow is filled, return to the area where the sphere meets the surface and push that contrast hard. This is the darkest part of the cast shadow — it's what makes the sphere feel grounded, not floating.

title: Shadow gradation — near to far
shortPrompt: Closest part of the shadow = darkest. Gradate outward to extend depth.
text: Finish by strengthening the shadow nearest to us, then gradate it lighter as it moves away. This near-to-far gradation stretches the perception of space — the shadow becomes the tool that pulls the eye into depth.

title: Build the light-gray halftone band
shortPrompt: Wrap a light gray band from terminator into the light side.
text: This is the halftone area — a band of value that extends from the terminator into the light side. Wrap it gently around the whole sphere. Switch to a lighter pencil (HB or 2H) — this is not a line, it's an entire surface that helps the light side transition naturally.

title: Cross-hatch to unify the tones
shortPrompt: Hatch against your previous stroke direction to blend values.
text: When you tone over your own strokes in the same direction, the result can feel rigid. Mrs. Dawn now adds strokes in the opposite direction — cross-hatching. This blending pass unifies the earlier tones into a softer, more continuous surface.

title: Soften the terminator into the shadow
shortPrompt: Don't leave the terminator as a hard line — connect it to the dark side.
text: A common mistake: drawing the terminator as a sharp, rigid line or block. Mrs. Dawn pushes that area repeatedly — not just darkening it, but also blending it gradually into the shadow side. The terminator should feel like a natural transition, not a wall.

title: It's a terminator BAND, not a line
shortPrompt: The dark-light boundary is a surface, not an edge.
text: Look carefully — Mrs. Dawn defines a clear terminator AREA, not a terminator line. This band acts as a bridge between the light side and the shadow side. It's what makes the sphere pop forward in 3D, and it's the key visual link between the two value zones.

title: Switch to 2B for stronger work
shortPrompt: Change pencils — now 2B for the deeper details.
text: Mrs. Dawn explicitly switches to a 2B pencil. The HB has carried you this far; the 2B will let you push the values that need to feel firmer and richer.

title: Radiate from the terminator outward
shortPrompt: Use 2B to spread values from the terminator into both light and dark.
text: With 2B, Mrs. Dawn strengthens transitions in both directions — from the terminator toward the light side, and from the terminator toward the dark side. This radiating gradient is what gives the sphere strong perspective. She also strengthens the cast shadow with the same pencil.

title: Bring out the blender
shortPrompt: Blender / tissue / napkin — softens the whole surface.
text: Mrs. Dawn introduces a blending tool — a blending stump if you have one, or a tissue or napkin works fine. This tool unifies and softens all the tones you've built up. The drawing should feel more like a smooth surface than a series of pencil strokes.

title: Follow your stroke direction
shortPrompt: Blend along the direction of your strokes — never randomly.
text: Important: when blending, follow the direction of your pencil strokes. Sweep gently in the same direction. Do not press hard, and do not blend randomly across the surface — that creates a muddy, dirty drawing. Light, directional sweeps only.

title: Optional: re-touch with HB
shortPrompt: Press strong tones back into the paper with light HB strokes.
text: This step is optional but recommended. Mrs. Dawn returns to the HB pencil and gently presses the strongest tones back into the paper. This subtly tightens the whole drawing and makes it feel more natural — less like raw pencil, more like a unified surface.

title: Position your drawing on the page
text: Notice how Mrs. Dawn places small marks for the cube's four outer edges before she draws anything else. The distance from these marks to the edge of the paper matters — too close to the edge feels cramped, too centered feels stiff. Take a moment: do you have your paper ready, with room around where the cube will sit?

title: Use your pencil as a measuring tool
text: Mrs. Dawn holds her pencil at arm's length to measure the cube's height. This is one of the most important habits in observational drawing — your pencil becomes a ruler. Try holding your pencil this way now: arm fully extended, one eye closed. Mark the height before you commit to any lines.

title: The top plane — parallel FIRST, then perspective
text: This is where most students go wrong. The top of the cube tilts away from us — but you need to draw it parallel first, then gently apply perspective. Don't try to "see the angle" right away. Draw the top edges horizontal, then carefully tilt them inward. Look at Mrs. Dawn's example: notice how subtle the perspective actually is.

title: See through the cube — internal framework
text: Mrs. Dawn draws the cube as if it were transparent — showing the edges you can't actually see. This isn't for show. Understanding the internal framework helps you feel the cube's 3D space. The back corners must align with the front corners. If your hidden edges look wrong, the visible ones will too.

title: Perspective lines: parallel before they converge
text: Same rule as the top plane — keep your perspective lines (and any diagonal/background lines) parallel first. THEN gently bring them inward toward the vanishing point. Going straight to "angled" without "parallel" first makes the cube look wonky. Slow it down. Parallel first. Tilt second.

title: 4B: Start from the darkest plane
shortPrompt: Use 4B and begin from the darkest side.
text: Lay in the darkest plane first. Keep the strokes moving in one direction so the tone stays clean and controlled.
learnerAction: Shade the darkest plane using one-direction strokes.
voiceoverEn: Start with a 4B pencil and build the darkest plane first. Keep all of your strokes moving in one direction so the shading feels clean and organized.

title: Change direction
shortPrompt: Overlay a second layer to build gradation.
text: Change the stroke direction and overlay the first layer. This creates a smoother gradation and a stronger sense of 3D depth.
learnerAction: Add a second layer in a new direction.
voiceoverEn: Now change direction and add a second layer over the first shading. This helps build a smoother transition and gives the form stronger depth.

title: Fully apply the dark plane
shortPrompt: Cover the whole dark side evenly.
text: Fully apply the dark tone across the entire plane. Keep the surface clean so the dark side feels solid and unified.
learnerAction: Evenly fill the full dark plane.
voiceoverEn: Now fully cover the dark plane. Try to keep the tone even across the whole side so it feels complete and well controlled.

title: Strengthen the light-dark edge
shortPrompt: Emphasize the boundary for stronger depth.
text: Darken the boundary between the light and dark planes. This edge makes the cube feel more solid and spatial.
voiceoverEn: Strengthen the edge between the light side and the dark side. This boundary is what helps the cube feel sharper and more three-dimensional.

title: Add the cast shadow
shortPrompt: Draw the shadow with clean, controlled strokes.
text: Add the cast shadow beside the cube and keep the shading direction consistent so the shadow feels tidy and believable.
learnerAction: Shade the cast shadow in one direction.
voiceoverEn: Now add the cast shadow. Keep the strokes moving in one direction here too, so the shadow stays clean and controlled.

title: 2B: Add the light-gray plane
shortPrompt: Use a lighter touch on the light-gray side.
text: Switch to a 2B pencil and lightly shade the lighter plane. Build contrast with the dark plane while keeping the transition smooth.
learnerAction: Lightly shade the light-gray plane with 2B.
voiceoverEn: Switch to a 2B pencil and shade the light gray plane with a lighter touch. Create contrast, but keep the transition into the dark plane soft.

title: HB: Unify the surface
shortPrompt: Sweep lightly to harmonize the tone.
text: Use HB to lightly sweep over the surface and unify the texture. This helps clean up rough marks and harmonize the plane.
learnerAction: Lightly sweep across the plane with HB.
voiceoverEn: Use an HB pencil to lightly sweep over the surface. This helps clean up rough strokes and makes the tone feel more unified.

title: Blend lightly
shortPrompt: Use a tissue or blender to soften the tone.
text: Use a tissue or blender to soften the graphite and create a smoother transition, while still keeping the form clear.
learnerAction: Blend the surface gently without losing the edges.
voiceoverEn: Now use a tissue or a blender to soften the graphite. Blend lightly so the tones transition smoothly, while the shape of the cube stays clear.

title: Edge dissolves — top plane emerges
shortPrompt: Watch the edge disappear into the background.
text: Notice how Mrs. Dawn's outer edge line gradually dissolves into the background — it no longer reads as a separate line. And look at the top plane: by strengthening the background, the top face suddenly appears much brighter. She didn't touch the top plane — she changed what surrounds it.
learnerAction: Look at your own drawing: can you soften one edge so it merges with the background?
voiceoverEn: Watch how the outer edge is slowly disappearing into the background. It no longer reads as a separate line. And notice the top plane — by darkening the background around it, the top has become much brighter without being touched.

title: Strengthen the shadow
shortPrompt: Push the shadow darker for stronger contrast.
text: Mrs. Dawn goes back into the shadow area and pushes it darker. This is deliberate — stronger shadow means stronger contrast, which means more convincing light. The light side doesn't change, but the shadow getting darker makes the light side look even brighter.
learnerAction: Deepen your core shadow with one or two more passes. Don't blend yet.
voiceoverEn: Now Mrs. Dawn strengthens the shadow area. By pushing the shadow darker, the contrast between light and dark becomes stronger — and that contrast is what makes the form feel three-dimensional.

title: Return to the terminator line
shortPrompt: Reinforce the terminator for stronger 3D.
text: Mrs. Dawn returns to the terminator — the boundary between light and shadow — and darkens it further. This is the key move: the terminator is the darkest area on the form itself (not the cast shadow). Strengthening it pushes the 3D effect dramatically. A soft terminator makes a sphere look flat; a firm one makes it pop.
learnerAction: Find your terminator line and add a few more strokes to darken just that belt.
voiceoverEn: Mrs. Dawn goes back to the terminator line — the boundary between light and shadow — and reinforces it. This is what creates the strongest sense of three-dimensional form. The darker the terminator, the more the sphere pops.

title: Natural tonal transition
shortPrompt: Tone flows left to right, top to bottom — dark to light.
text: Notice the overall tonal map now: from left to right, from top to bottom, values transition naturally from dark to light. This isn't accidental — it's planned. Each area of the sphere flows smoothly into the next. There are no sudden jumps in value, no hard edges where there shouldn't be any.
learnerAction: Step back from your drawing. Can you see a smooth gradient from dark to light? Look for any jumps that need softening.
voiceoverEn: Look at the full sphere now. From left to right, from top to bottom, the tone transitions naturally from dark to light. This gradual flow is what makes the form feel unified and real.

title: Blend to unify
shortPrompt: Use a blender or tissue — gently sweep along the strokes.
text: Now Mrs. Dawn uses a blender to soften and unify the surface. If you don't have a blending stump, a tissue or cotton bud (maccan) works just as well. The key: follow the direction of your pencil strokes, sweep very lightly. This is not about erasing tone — it's about making the transitions smoother and the surface feel more continuous.
learnerAction: Use a blender, tissue, or cotton bud. Follow your stroke direction. Sweep lightly — don't press.
voiceoverEn: Now blend the surface gently. A blending stump, tissue, or cotton bud all work. Follow the direction of your strokes and sweep very lightly. This softens the transitions and unifies the whole surface.

title: Measure left & right with your pencil
shortPrompt: Use your pencil as a tool to check symmetry.
text: Just like we practiced before — use your pencil as a measuring tool. Compare left to right so the cylinder begins with a stable, balanced frame from the very first stroke.

title: Mark top, bottom, left, right
shortPrompt: Frame the cylinder like building a house.
text: The teacher places dots above, below, and on each side. These four points define how much of the page the cylinder will fill. Check the gap to the paper edge — too big or too small and the composition fails.

title: Box the cylinder in a rectangle
shortPrompt: Draw the outer rectangle that holds the entire form.
text: The teacher draws a long rectangle around where the cylinder will sit. This rectangle gives the cylinder a clear, direct answer for its size — no guessing.

title: Check that top & bottom match
shortPrompt: Pencil-measure to verify equal areas above and below.
text: The teacher finds a point and measures with the pencil — checking whether the top section matches the area of the bottom. Equal proportions = a believable cylinder.

title: Frame where the front curve will sit
shortPrompt: Build sub-frames above and below to locate the ellipses.
text: The teacher draws specific guide frames at the top and bottom. These tell you exactly where the front curve should arc through. With this scaffolding, your pencil moves with confidence.

title: Cut with straight tangents — not curves yet
shortPrompt: Draw the upper edge as a series of short straight lines.
text: Just like with the sphere — circles and ellipses are very hard for beginners. The teacher uses straight tangent cuts first to find the right angles, then softens them into a curve.

title: Find the bottom curve points
shortPrompt: Mark high and low points of the bottom arc, symmetrically.
text: The teacher locates the starting points for the bottom ellipse. Find the highest and lowest points of the curve — and they must be perfectly left-right symmetric.

title: Keep top & bottom curves parallel
shortPrompt: Both arcs must curve downward at the same angle.
text: The bottom curve is almost finished. Common mistake: students draw it too flat. The top and bottom curves must arc downward in parallel — if either becomes too flat, the perspective breaks.

title: Start the terminator with 2B
shortPrompt: Use a 2B pencil — vertical strokes along the cylinder.
text: Switch to a 2B pencil. The terminator on a cylinder runs vertically — let your pencil strokes follow that direction, sweeping down along the form. Keep it light at first; you can deepen it later.

title: Sketch the cast shadow at the same time
shortPrompt: Follow the shape of the cylinder's cast reflection on the surface.
text: Now draw the cast shadow on the table — its outline follows the shape the cylinder casts on the surface. Develop the terminator and the shadow together. They belong to one connected system, not two separate things.

title: Rough-shade the dark side with 2B
shortPrompt: Quick vertical strokes across the terminator + dark zone.
text: Take a 2B pencil and lay down a quick pass of tone across the dark side, vertical strokes following the cylinder's direction. This is rough shading — it doesn't need to be pretty. Just lay it in fast and uniform.

title: Always develop the shadow at the same time
shortPrompt: Cast shadow + cylinder dark side = one family.
text: The cylinder and its shadow always develop together — never separately. Use the same stroke direction so the eye reads them as one unified scene.

title: Strengthen the shadow contrast
shortPrompt: Go back into the shadow to push the value.
text: Return to the cast shadow and deepen it. This stronger contrast anchors the cylinder to the surface and gives the whole drawing more visual punch.

title: Add horizontal strokes — bridge for later
shortPrompt: Stiff lines kill the form. Crossing strokes build a bridge.
text: Even though we strengthened the terminator, it shouldn't look stiff. Add horizontal strokes across it now — these will become the bridge to the light side later, making the eventual transition feel natural.

title: Blend with paper, following the strokes
shortPrompt: Use rolled paper as a blender — same direction as your strokes.
text: Just like with the sphere and cube, take a piece of rolled paper (or tissue) and blend along the direction of your strokes. This unifies the tone without losing the form direction.

title: Switch to 3B — push contrast
shortPrompt: Same direction strokes, darker pencil.
text: Now switch to a 3B pencil. Push the value contrast further — but keep the strokes going the same direction. No messy criss-crossing.

title: Vertical strokes turn the line into a band
shortPrompt: The terminator stops being a line — it becomes a zone.
text: Lay more vertical strokes through the dark side. The terminator stops reading as a single line and becomes a band of value — that's what makes the form feel three-dimensional.

title: Horizontal strokes again — keep building the bridge
shortPrompt: Cross-hatch the band to soften toward the light side.
text: Add another pass of horizontal strokes. We're building the bridge between dark and light — the gentler the transition, the more believable the form.

title: Shadow — denser, cleaner strokes
shortPrompt: Not rough sketching anymore — controlled hatching.
text: Return to the cast shadow one more time. This time the strokes are denser, more deliberate, more controlled. The whole drawing becomes cleaner and more crisp.

title: Switch to HB or 2H for the light side
shortPrompt: Light pencil for the half-light zone — choose by your touch.
text: Switch to HB or 2H — pick based on how heavy your touch is. Heavy hand → 2H. Light hand → HB. Lightly start hatching the half-light area with vertical, parallel strokes.

title: Build the bridge: dark → light gradation
shortPrompt: HB or 2H continues the gradation from terminator to highlight.
text: This is the key move: the gradation from dark to light. Use HB if your touch is light, 2H if your touch is heavy. Smooth, continuous transition wraps the cylinder.

title: Use 2H to refine details
shortPrompt: Switch to 2H for fine carving.
text: For more refined detail work, switch to 2H. The lighter graphite lets you sharpen and define without darkening areas you don't want darker.

title: Diagonal strokes on the dark side with 2B
shortPrompt: Now diagonal hatching builds the gradation from the shadow side.
text: Bring 2B back. Build the gradation in the dark side with diagonal strokes going up. The change in stroke direction reinforces the form's curve.

title: Light side gets 2H treatment
shortPrompt: Continue refining the light side with 2H.
text: Use 2H to add the finishing touches on the light side. Strokes stay parallel and gentle — this is the lightest value zone.

title: Outer edge: drawn but not too sharp
shortPrompt: The far edge is behind — softer than the front terminator.
text: The outer (far) edge needs tone, but it shouldn't be as hard as the terminator. Remember: the terminator is in front, the outer edge is behind. The closer thing is sharper; the farther thing is softer.

title: Clean diagonal shading pass
shortPrompt: Tidy diagonal strokes — even, parallel, controlled.
text: Use diagonal strokes for a clean shading pass. You should see a tidy, parallel band of hatching — this is the controlled finish that separates a polished drawing from a sketch.

title: Switch back to 2B
shortPrompt: One more pass with 2B for value depth.
text: Switch back to 2B to add some final depth where needed. Brief and surgical — only the spots that need pushing.

title: Final blending pass
shortPrompt: Blend everything together with paper or tissue.
text: Final blending — use paper or tissue to unify the surface one last time. After this, the dark side of the cylinder reads as a continuous, three-dimensional form.

title: Straight lines block in the shape
Find the tilt before the outline
shortPrompt: Compare the guide lines before adding detail.
text: The teacher is finding the direction and overall shape before adding any shading. Notice the tilted guide lines. Compare their angles, and keep your construction marks light.
voiceoverEn: The teacher is finding the direction and overall shape before adding any shading. Notice the tilted guide lines. Compare their angles, and keep your construction marks light.

title: Turn corners into soft curves
shortPrompt: Foil has volume: let the edges bend.
text: Pause to compare the outline with the finished balloon beside the video. The edges bend inward between the points. Use gentle curves instead of making every edge a straight line.
voiceoverEn: Pause to compare the outline with the finished balloon beside the video. The edges bend inward between the points. Use gentle curves instead of making every edge a straight line.

title: Separate the seam from the outline
shortPrompt: Look for the narrow rim inside the edge.
text: Look closely at the rim just inside the balloon outline. This seam is separate from the outer edge. Keep that narrow space visible; it will help the balloon feel like inflated foil.
voiceoverEn: Look closely at the rim just inside the balloon outline. This seam is separate from the outer edge. Keep that narrow space visible; it will help the balloon feel like inflated foil.

title: Let folds turn toward the centre
shortPrompt: Follow each fold’s direction.
text: These small inward curves describe folds in the foil. Notice how they turn from the rim toward the centre. Draw the folds you can see, keeping them light before the shading begins.
voiceoverEn: These small inward curves describe folds in the foil. Notice how they turn from the rim toward the centre. Draw the folds you can see, keeping them light before the shading begins.

title: Compare height and width
shortPrompt: Keep the cone balanced around its centre.
text: Before adding detail, compare the height with the base width. Use light marks to set the limits. The tip should sit above the centre of the base, so neither side feels heavier.
voiceoverEn: Before adding detail, compare the height with the base width. Use light marks to set the limits. The tip should sit above the centre of the base, so neither side feels heavier.

title: Check both sides of the axis
shortPrompt: Compare left and right before joining them.
text: Look at the small width marks on either side of the centre line. Compare those distances before drawing the sides. A small correction now is easier than repairing a shaded cone.
voiceoverEn: Look at the small width marks on either side of the centre line. Compare those distances before drawing the sides. A small correction now is easier than repairing a shaded cone.

title: Connect the tip to the base
shortPrompt: Light straight guides first.
text: The teacher connects the top point to the two outer limits of the base. Keep these construction lines light. They establish the overall taper before the curved base is refined.
voiceoverEn: The teacher connects the top point to the two outer limits of the base. Keep these construction lines light. They establish the overall taper before the curved base is refined.

title: Round the base into an ellipse
shortPrompt: Avoid sharp corners at the ends.
text: The circular base appears as an ellipse from this viewpoint. Notice the curve across the front. Round the ends gently instead of closing them into sharp points.
voiceoverEn: The circular base appears as an ellipse from this viewpoint. Notice the curve across the front. Round the ends gently instead of closing them into sharp points.

title: Lift the construction marks
shortPrompt: Erase gently; keep the useful outline.
text: The teacher is using an eraser to lift construction marks near the base. Remove only the guides you no longer need. Keep the curved outline readable and avoid rubbing hard enough to damage the paper.
voiceoverEn: The teacher is using an eraser to lift construction marks near the base. Remove only the guides you no longer need. Keep the curved outline readable and avoid rubbing hard enough to damage the paper.

title: Check the front curve
shortPrompt: One smooth curve, not a flat bottom.
text: Pause and compare the front edge of the base with your drawing. It curves smoothly across the form. Keep that curve consistent so the cone feels round and rests naturally on the surface.
voiceoverEn: Pause and compare the front edge of the base with your drawing. It curves smoothly across the form. Keep that curve consistent so the cone feels round and rests naturally on the surface.

title: Place the light–shadow boundary
shortPrompt: The shadow narrows toward the tip.
text: This inner line maps where the cone turns away from the light. Notice how it approaches the tip. It is a guide for a tonal transition, not a dark outline to leave on the finished cone.
voiceoverEn: This inner line maps where the cone turns away from the light. Notice how it approaches the tip. It is a guide for a tonal transition, not a dark outline to leave on the finished cone.

title: Connect the cast shadow
shortPrompt: The shadow begins at the contact point.
text: The teacher shades the cast shadow beside the base. Keep the shadow connected to the cone, rather than floating away from it. Build the tone with several light passes.
voiceoverEn: The teacher shades the cast shadow beside the base. Keep the shadow connected to the cone, rather than floating away from it. Build the tone with several light passes.

title: Establish the dark side
shortPrompt: Keep the light area clear.
text: Build a clear dark area on the side that turns away from the light. Compare this with the still-light area. Keep the difference readable before adding softer middle tones.
voiceoverEn: Build a clear dark area on the side that turns away from the light. Compare this with the still-light area. Keep the difference readable before adding softer middle tones.

title: Layer your pencil marks
shortPrompt: Several light passes give you control.
text: Watch how the teacher returns to the same area with light strokes. Build the dark gradually instead of pressing hard in one pass. This keeps the paper workable and the tone easier to adjust.
voiceoverEn: Watch how the teacher returns to the same area with light strokes. Build the dark gradually instead of pressing hard in one pass. This keeps the paper workable and the tone easier to adjust.

title: Let the marks follow the taper
shortPrompt: The form narrows as it rises.
text: Near the tip, the shaded area becomes narrower. Keep your marks controlled as they approach that point. Avoid a heavy knot of graphite at the top.
voiceoverEn: Near the tip, the shaded area becomes narrower. Keep your marks controlled as they approach that point. Avoid a heavy knot of graphite at the top.

title: Build the middle tone
shortPrompt: Bridge light and shadow gradually.
text: Now look between the light area and the darker band. These middle tones help the surface turn toward the shadow. Add them gradually so the cone does not look like two flat cut-out shapes.
voiceoverEn: Now look between the light area and the darker band. These middle tones help the surface turn toward the shadow. Add them gradually so the cone does not look like two flat cut-out shapes.

title: Soften the transition
shortPrompt: Blend with pencil strokes before rubbing.
text: Use overlapping light pencil marks to connect neighbouring tones. Keep the light area lighter, and let the transition become smoother. Softening a transition does not mean making the whole cone the same grey.
voiceoverEn: Use overlapping light pencil marks to connect neighbouring tones. Keep the light area lighter, and let the transition become smoother. Softening a transition does not mean making the whole cone the same grey.

title: Keep the base grounded
shortPrompt: Compare the contact edge with the side.
text: Look at the darker contact along the bottom. It helps the cone sit on the table. Keep this accent controlled, rather than outlining the entire cone with an equally dark line.
voiceoverEn: Look at the darker contact along the bottom. It helps the cone sit on the table. Keep this accent controlled, rather than outlining the entire cone with an equally dark line.

title: Use the background to reveal the edge
shortPrompt: Dark beside light makes the form clearer.
text: The teacher adds tone outside the light side of the cone. This contrast helps the light edge become visible without a thick outline. Keep the background marks outside the form.
voiceoverEn: The teacher adds tone outside the light side of the cone. This contrast helps the light edge become visible without a thick outline. Keep the background marks outside the form.

title: Keep broad marks consistent
shortPrompt: Build an even surrounding tone.
text: Notice the broad diagonal strokes around the cone. Use a consistent direction and gentle pressure to establish the surrounding tone. Check that the cone still stands out clearly.
voiceoverEn: Notice the broad diagonal strokes around the cone. Use a consistent direction and gentle pressure to establish the surrounding tone. Check that the cone still stands out clearly.

title: Check the cast-shadow shape
shortPrompt: Keep it attached; soften farther away.
text: Compare the cast shadow with the base. Its darkest contact stays near the object, while the outer area can soften. Avoid turning it into a hard, equally dark border.
voiceoverEn: Compare the cast shadow with the base. Its darkest contact stays near the object, while the outer area can soften. Avoid turning it into a hard, equally dark border.

title: Compare the whole value pattern
shortPrompt: Light side, turning tone, dark side.
text: Step back for a moment. Compare the light area, the middle transition, and the shadow. The background should support those differences, not compete with the cone.
voiceoverEn: Step back for a moment. Compare the light area, the middle transition, and the shadow. The background should support those differences, not compete with the cone.
